# Education in Poland
Education in Poland is compulsory and typically begins with primary school (szkoła podstawowa), which children start at age six or seven. Since reforms enacted in 2017, primary education lasts eight years, replacing the previous system of six years of primary school followed by three years of junior high (gimnazjum), which was abolished by 2019. The junior high previously provided lower secondary education covering subjects like Polish, history, foreign languages, sciences, technology, and religion. At the end, students underwent evaluations including exams in humanities, science, and languages.
Upper secondary education in Poland offers several paths: general secondary schools (liceum) lasting four years culminating in the Matura exam for university admission; technical schools (technikum) lasting five years that combine vocational training with Matura preparation; basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa) offering three years of vocational education with a certificate of competence, with options to pursue Matura through additional schooling; and profiled general secondary schools (liceum profilowane) providing vocational education aligned with specified economic activities. Mentally or physically handicapped students attend special schools preparing them for the Matura. Poland implements the Bologna scheme in tertiary education with three-year bachelor’s degrees followed by two-year master’s, with doctoral studies typically taking three years. Teacher training and vocational post-secondary schooling are also part of the system, with grading at university level on a scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest).
